content: 1. All individuals in neighboring households within the village or hamlet surrounding the residence of the index case should be screened for fever lasting two or more weeks. This screening is to be conducted by staff from the Primary Health Center (PHC), Health Post (HP), Urban Health Center (UHC), or by trained health workers and volunteers. 2. A patient referral form must be completed for suspected cases, and the patient should be referred to the nearest PHC, district hospital, zonal hospital, or upazila hospital for confirmation of kala-azar diagnosis. 3. A list of all patients referred for confirmation of kala-azar diagnosis must be maintained for record-keeping and follow-up purposes. 4. The PHC, district, zonal, or upazila hospital staff must be informed about the patients referred for kala-azar diagnosis to ensure proper coordination and management. 5. Records of index case findings and related activities must be maintained and reported to the district or upazila level for monitoring and validation purposes. 6. All patients referred by health workers after index case-based searches must have their diagnosis confirmed at the appropriate health facility. 7. Ensure that all confirmed kala-azar patients are promptly initiated on treatment. 8. Monitor treatment compliance and assess for any side effects during the course of therapy. 9. Ensure timely disbursement of wage-loss compensation to kala-azar and post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) patients in India and Nepal. 10. Ensure timely payment of incentives to NGO health workers or health volunteers for patient follow-up activities in India. 11. Maintain an adequate supply of drugs and diagnostic tools at hospitals based on the number of kala-azar cases reported. 12. Monthly reports from PHCs, districts, or upazilas on the number of kala-azar cases and drug distribution must be assessed to ensure proper resource allocation. 13. Drugs and diagnostic supplies should be distributed to PHCs, districts, or UHCs based on the number of reported kala-azar cases. 14. Supervision and monitoring reports should be used to evaluate the effectiveness of index case-finding activities. 15. Public and NGO health workers must be informed about patients diagnosed and started on kala-azar or PKDL treatment to ensure compliance and address any side effects. 16. The camp-based approach for active case detection of new kala-azar cases should be implemented in high-endemic areas, ideally twice a year, as defined by each country. 17. The program manager of the kala-azar elimination program at the district or upazila level is responsible for implementing camp detection strategies. 18. Materials required for camp activities include rk39 test kits, lancets, gloves, general medicines (antipyretics, antibiotics, antidiarrheals, antimalarials), rapid diagnostic kits for malaria (if applicable), patient referral forms, lab investigation forms, camp registers, IEC materials, and emergency drugs. 19. Pre-camp preparatory activities include identifying high-incidence areas, conducting planning meetings, preparing a micro-action plan, scheduling camps, estimating logistics requirements, and organizing supervision and monitoring plans. 20. On the day of the camp, a team comprising a medical officer, lab technician, nurse, and community volunteers should organize activities, register patients, and conduct examinations for fever lasting two or more weeks, splenomegaly, and skin lesions. 21. Positive rk39 test results should lead to the completion of a case referral form, and the patient should be referred to the appropriate health facility for treatment and follow-up. 22. Suspected PKDL cases with positive rk39 tests and a history of kala-azar treatment should be referred to a district or higher-level hospital for confirmation and treatment initiation. 23. Patients with severe kala-azar or co-infections should be referred to an appropriate hospital for specialized care. 24. Proper disposal of bio-waste generated during the camp must be ensured. 25. Post-camp activities at the PHC level include maintaining camp records, managing patient-specific drug boxes, ensuring follow-up for referred patients, and assessing camp outcomes such as attendance, diagnostic tests performed, and treatment initiation. 26. Monthly camp activity reports should be submitted to the district level, and timely payment of incentives to health workers and wage-loss compensation to patients must be ensured. 27. At the district level, camp reports should be assessed, and drugs and diagnostics should be supplied based on the number of reported cases. Supervision and monitoring reports should be used to evaluate camp activities. 28. At the village level, NGO and health workers must be informed about diagnosed patients to ensure treatment compliance and address side effects. 29. The incentive-based approach for active case detection of kala-azar and PKDL cases should be implemented in low-endemic areas on an ongoing basis throughout the year. 30. Preparatory activities for the incentive-based approach include identifying endemic areas, training health workers, preparing supervision and monitoring plans, and managing funds for incentives. 31. Health workers and volunteers should screen individuals for fever lasting two or more weeks, complete referral forms, and refer patients to the nearest health facility for confirmation of kala-azar diagnosis. 32. Post-incentive-based activities include confirming diagnoses, initiating treatment, monitoring compliance and side effects, maintaining records, and ensuring timely payment of incentives and wage-loss compensation. 33. A country report or dossier documenting all evidence supporting the elimination of kala-azar should include historical perspectives, epidemiology, program strategies, surveillance systems, and treatment protocols. This report should be based on a thorough review of data, reports, and interviews with health officials.
